alt: A time scale from 1460 to 1560 with two bands: Granada (1482-1492) and Mexico and Peru (1519-1551). Dated events below run from the marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand in 1469 and the Inquisition in 1478 to 1492, when Granada was entered in January and terms were agreed with Columbus in April, then Cortés in 1519, Tenochtitlan in 1521, Atahualpa's capture in 1532, the New Laws of 1542 and the Valladolid debate of 1550-51.
caption: 1492 links the two case studies: Granada in January, Columbus in April.

alt: Before the 1480s Granada survived by paying tribute to a Castile that was often divided. Two changes broke the balance: the Christian kingdoms were united by the marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand (1469) and the succession war (1475-1479), and Granada was divided by a dynastic struggle among Abu'l-Hasan Ali, Boabdil and al-Zaghal. Both lead to the war of 1482-1492, driven by crusade and royal authority.
caption: Christian unity and Granadan division ended two centuries of balance.

alt: A vertical timeline: Alhama seized in 1482, Boabdil captured at Lucena in 1483 and released as a vassal, Ronda and Málaga taken in 1485-1487 with artillery, Baza and al-Zaghal's surrender in 1489, the siege from Santa Fe in 1490-1491, the Capitulations in November 1491 and the city's surrender on 2 January 1492.
caption: Artillery sieges and Granada's civil war brought the city down in ten years.

alt: A downward chain: the Capitulations of November 1491 promise Muslims their religion, mosques, property and law; Archbishop Talavera seeks conversion by persuasion; from 1499 Cisneros presses mass baptisms, provoking revolts in 1499-1501; in 1502 Muslims in Castile must convert or leave. A side column adds the Inquisition in Castile from 1478 and the Alhambra Decree of March 1492 expelling Jews who would not convert.
caption: Persuasion gave way to compulsion within ten years of the Capitulations.

alt: A central circle, the Spanish conquest, linked to five factors: indigenous allies such as the Totonacs and Tlaxcalans, epidemics including smallpox, the interpreters Malinche and Aguilar, the Inca civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa, and Spanish actions such as seizing rulers and building brigantines. A note summarises Restall's argument that indigenous allies, disease and politics shaped the outcome.
caption: Allies, disease and indigenous politics matter as much as Spanish arms.

alt: Two columns of events. Mexico: Cortés sails from Cuba in 1519, enters Tenochtitlan in November 1519 and takes Moctezuma hostage; after Alvarado's massacre in 1520 the city rises and the Spanish flee; smallpox strikes; Tenochtitlan is taken in August 1521. Peru: the Inca civil war; Atahualpa captured at Cajamarca in November 1532 and executed in 1533; Manco Inca rebels in 1536; Almagro is executed in 1538 and Pizarro assassinated in 1541.
caption: Mexico fell in two years; Peru was taken quickly but fought over for a decade.

alt: Two sources on the fall of Tenochtitlan, a letter from Cortés to Charles V and a later indigenous account, are compared row by row with two-way arrows. Similarity: both say the siege destroyed the city. Differences: the letter credits Spanish courage and divine favour while the indigenous account stresses disease and hunger; the letter treats allies as auxiliaries while the indigenous account names them as fighting their old overlords.
caption: Link the two sources in every sentence: similarities and differences side by side.
